title: Carved hazel grain scoop
subtitle: Green-wood spoon-carving: a deep scoop for dry goods
excerpt: A deep hazel scoop for flour, sugar, oats, or seed. Wider and deeper than a spoon, with a flat base that sits level on a shelf. Hazel cleaves cleanly into the wide billet this project needs, and the green wood carves quickly with an axe and sloyd knife.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the treen scoop form; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the axe-to-knife blank progression on wider billets.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content.
A short length of split timber, ready to be worked into a blank.
The rough-shaped piece of wood from which the finished scoop is carved.
The curvature of a gouge cutting edge, numbered from 1 (flat) to 11 (deep U). A No. 7 is a medium-deep curve.
A curved-bladed knife for hollowing the bowl or interior of a carved piece.

content.text: A grain scoop is a deeper, wider version of a spoon, typically 10 cm or more across the bowl face and deep enough to hold a generous cup of flour or oats. Hazel splits into wide flat billets readily from a coppice pole of 8, 10 cm diameter. The work is the same axe-to-knife progression as a spoon, but the bowl hollow is wide enough that a gouge or hook knife with a large radius is needed to clean the bottom. The scoop sits flat on a shelf or in a pot; the base is carved flat for stability.
This project uses
green wood
. Source a hazel pole of 10 cm diameter or greater. The pith should be at least 2 cm from the intended bowl base for structural strength.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
What you need
Wood
One hazel
billet

, 22 cm long and at least 10 cm in diameter. Split in quarters to give a wide flat blank, the quarter-split piece will be roughly 10 cm wide and 5 cm deep, which is exactly the shape needed. Hazel is food-safe under raw linseed oil. Birch or lime work as alternatives for a lighter finished scoop.
Tools
Carving axe for rough shaping the blank from the split section.
Sloyd knife for handle and outside shaping.
Hook knife, large, for the bowl hollow.
Gouge, sweep No. 7, 12 mm (optional): useful for cleaning the flat base of the bowl interior that the hook knife cannot reach.
Leather strop.
180-grit sandpaper (optional for bowl interior).
Raw linseed oil.
Workspace
A low bench or carving stool. The axe work needs a stable splitting block; the knife work can be done on the lap with a leather apron.
The work
Step 1: Split the billet and rough out with the axe
Quarter-split the hazel pole using a froe and mallet or a splitting axe and wedge. Select the best quarter, straight grain, away from knots. The
blank

will be used with the pith side as the inside of the scoop (the pith wood is softer and easier to hollow). Mark the scoop profile: bowl roughly 10 cm long and 8 cm wide, handle 10 cm. Use the carving axe to rough out the plan shape, working with the grain from the bowl toward the handle tip. The axe removes large waste quickly; switch to the sloyd knife when within 5 mm of the pencil line.
Step 2: Thin the blank and shape the back
Use
push cuts

to reduce the back of the bowl to about 12 mm thickness at the rim and 15 mm at the base of the bowl (the flat bottom). The scoop base is meant to be flat, carve the back so it sits level without rocking before hollowing begins. This is easier to achieve in green wood before the hollow is cut.
Step 3: Hollow the bowl

Use the hook knife, large, to hollow the interior. Begin at the rim and work toward the centre. The large hook knife sweeps across the wide bowl face in arcs. For the flat area at the base of the bowl interior, use the
gouge sweep
No. 7 with mallet taps to clean what the hook knife cannot reach. A
hook knife
always cuts best with the grain running toward the blade from the far side of the bowl toward the near; if the hook catches, rotate the piece and cut from the other direction.
Step 4: Shape the handle
Use push cuts and
thumb-pivot cuts

to taper the handle to a comfortable grip, roughly 12 mm at the shoulder, 10 mm at the end. A small thumb notch on the underside of the handle, about 4 cm from the bowl shoulder, improves the grip for scooping.
Finishing

Let the scoop dry for two to three days, standing upright with the bowl opening down so any moisture can leave evenly. Apply raw linseed oil inside and out. Soak for one hour, wipe off the surplus. Repeat after twenty-four hours. Cure for two weeks before using with food.
Variations
Smaller coffee scoop: same method, half the scale, from a hazel branch 6 cm across. No axe needed, a sloyd knife and hook knife small are sufficient.
Left-handed: the scoop is symmetrical; no adjustment needed.
Care
Wipe clean rather than washing if used for dry goods, flour, oats, seed. If washed, dry immediately and re-oil after washing.

attrs.symptom: The flat scoop base rocks after drying
attrs.cause: The base was not made flat before hollowing, and the wood distorted slightly as it dried
attrs.fix: Place the scoop base down on a flat sheet of 80-grit sandpaper and work in small circles to flatten it. A few passes is usually enough.

attrs.symptom: The hook knife stalls in the deep bowl interior
attrs.cause: Cutting against the grain in the bowl base or blade is dull
attrs.fix: Strop the hook knife first. Then rotate the piece so the cut goes with the grain, always toward the blade from the far side of the bowl. For the very bottom, switch to the gouge with mallet taps.
